items.title: Computational and experimental strategies for functional validation of non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer.
items.summary: Journal: Functional & integrative genomics. Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterised by extensive genomic heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. Although recurrent coding mutations in key driver genes have been well researched, large-scale sequencing studies have identified a broad array of non-coding variants which may contribute to tumorigenesis by interfering with gene regulatory mechanisms. However, understanding the functional significance of these variants remains a major challenge due to their abundance and the complexity of non-coding regulatory structures. This review outlines current computational and experimental techniques to identify, prioritise, and functionally validate non-coding variants in PDAC. We discuss in silico methods including genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapping, colocalisation, machine learning-driven functional annotation, and the use of established computational tools, in addition to epigenomic profiling technologies including, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and CUT&RUN which define regulatory landscapes. We also emphasise new AI-based methods involving radiogenomics, AI imaging analysis and data integration, which provides novel potential to link genomic variation with phenotypic and imaging characteristics. Additionally, we highlight experimental validation techniques including reporter assays, electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), chromatin conformation capture methods, and CRISPR-based perturbation systems used to study variant functionality. Together, these complementary approaches establish a framework for correlating non-coding variation to regulatory mechanisms in PDAC.
items.headline: Computational and experimental strategies for functional validation of non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer
items.brief: This review addresses the challenge of interpreting numerous non-coding variants identified in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) by outlining computational and experimental methods for their functional validation. It covers in silico techniques like GWAS fine-mapping, colocalization, and machine learning-driven annotation, alongside epigenomic profiling methods such as ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq to define regulatory elements. The approach aims to prioritize variants that impact gene regulation and contribute to tumorigenesis.
items.why: It directly tackles functional interpretation of non-coding regulatory variants in cancer genomics, a key problem in computational genomics and epigenomics with broad relevance.

items.title: Artificial intelligence aids multi-omics data integration in cancer drug discovery and development: from targets to drug synergy.
items.summary: Journal: Acta pharmacologica Sinica. Abstract: The emergence of multi-omics technologies has enabled the integration of genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data to characterize the molecular complexity of cancer. Single-cell and spatial profiling further resolve intratumoral heterogeneity, cell-cell interactions, and the microenvironmental determinants of therapeutic responses. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) provides computational approaches for integrating these heterogeneous data types across target identification, drug response prediction, toxicity assessment, and drug-combination modeling. Across these domains, the available evidence indicates that multi-omics integration is most beneficial when the included layers provide complementary biological information; that single-cell and spatial omics analyses reveal treatment-resistant populations and niches but remain largely research-grade and thus not ready for routine clinical deployment; and that although foundation models support some representation-learning tasks, their advantages in perturbation-response prediction require confirmation via stringent evaluation. By distinguishing externally validated advances from retrospective proof-of-concept studies, we provide a practical framework for evaluating the translational readiness of AI-driven multi-omics tools in precision oncology.
items.headline: Artificial intelligence aids multi-omics data integration in cancer drug discovery and development: from targets to drug synergy
items.brief: This article reviews how AI methods integrate multi-omics data (genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, metabolomic) to characterize cancer complexity and improve drug discovery and development. It highlights that combining complementary omics layers enhances biological insight, and that single-cell and spatial omics reveal treatment-resistant populations, though these remain mostly research-grade. Foundation models support some representation learning but have limited advantages in perturbation prediction currently.
items.why: It surveys AI-driven multi-omics integration approaches relevant to cancer genomics and epigenomics, informing computational strategies for complex biological data fusion.

items.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica.
items.summary: Journal: Science advances. Abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.
items.headline: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
items.brief: Using machine learning and explainable AI, this study analyzes genomic and epigenomic features to classify genes by subgenome identity in maize and Brassica rapa. It finds recombination rate as the most influential feature, interconnected with chromatin marks like H3K9ac and H3K27ac, accessible chromatin regions, and transposon density. These factors collectively predict biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring after polyploidy, linking 3D genome architecture and evolutionary divergence.
items.why: It applies interpretable ML to integrate chromatin and genomic features, elucidating regulatory and evolutionary mechanisms in plant polyploid genomes, relevant to chromatin and regulatory element studies.

items.title: Young children engage in choice-relative moral reasoning.
items.summary: Journal: Journal of experimental child psychology. Abstract: A central challenge in moral reasoning is evaluating actions not only by their outcomes, but also by the alternatives that were available at the time of choice. The present study examined whether preschool-age children engage in this form of choice-relative moral reasoning. Using a child-friendly version of the trolley problem, 3- to 5-year-old children (N = 124, 51% girls) judged a protagonist who moved a barrier to protect three children's cookies from being eaten by a mean squirrel. Children typically judged this action as morally good when no better alternative was available, even when it caused harm to another child. However, they judged the same action as morally bad when a non-harmful alternative was available but not chosen. These findings suggest that preschool-age children evaluate actions in light of available alternatives rather than solely on the basis of outcomes. Thus, even young children appear to consider what else could have been done when making moral judgments.
items.headline: Young children engage in choice-relative moral reasoning
items.brief: This study shows that preschool children (ages 3-5) evaluate moral actions not only by outcomes but also by the alternatives available at the time of choice. Using a child-friendly trolley problem, children judged an action as morally good when no better alternative existed, but as morally bad when a non-harmful alternative was available but not chosen. This indicates that even young children consider the context of available choices in moral judgments.
items.why: It provides experimental evidence on early developmental aspects of moral reasoning and decision-making, relevant to evolutionary psychology and cognitive neuroscience.

items.title: From animal behavior to human perioperative neurocognitive disorders: Translational boundaries of the gut-brain axis.
items.summary: Journal: Behavioural brain research. Abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND), including postoperative delirium (POD), delayed neurocognitive recovery (DNR), and postoperative neurocognitive disorder, are common after surgery in older adults, and the gut-brain axis has been proposed as a contributing pathway. Most mechanistic support rests on rodent behavioral assays, yet these endpoints and human clinical diagnoses are routinely treated as interchangeable. This critical narrative review examines that translational boundary. PND is used here as a clinically consequential test case for a broader behavioral-neuroscience problem: how animal behavioral phenotypes, microbiome-associated signals, and intervention effects should be translated into human diagnostic constructs. A structured search identified and appraised the principal evidence rather than an exhaustive synthesis; no formal risk-of-bias or certainty-of-evidence assessment was performed. Evidence was separated into human perioperative studies reporting a neurocognitive outcome with either a measured gut-brain exposure or a gut-directed intervention; those reporting gut-brain change without a cognitive outcome; perioperative preclinical evidence; and indirect non-perioperative evidence. The retrieved human perioperative evidence spans observational cohorts across gastric, orthopedic, spinal and cardiac surgery, multi-omic and metabolomic cohorts, and randomized perioperative probiotic trials reporting lower rates of study-defined cognitive outcomes. It nonetheless remains heterogeneous and largely single-center, with modest event numbers, inconsistent sampling and assessment, and limited external validation. Mechanistic support still comes mainly from perioperative rodent models using water maze, fear-conditioning, recognition-memory, and delirium-like readouts, which measure narrow, species-specific capacities and are not diagnostic equivalents of POD, DNR, or postoperative neurocognitive disorder. Microbiome-mediated causation is unproven, and cross-species endpoint alignment remains a central route to improved translation.
items.headline: From animal behavior to human perioperative neurocognitive disorders: Translational boundaries of the gut-brain axis
items.brief: This narrative review examines the translational challenges in linking rodent behavioral assays and microbiome studies to human perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND), including delirium and cognitive decline after surgery. It highlights that animal phenotypes and human clinical diagnoses are often treated interchangeably despite differences, and calls for careful interpretation of gut-brain axis mechanisms across species. The review emphasizes the need for improved translational frameworks to understand PND pathophysiology.
items.why: It critically evaluates the translational validity of animal models for neurocognitive disorders linked to microbiome and brain interactions, relevant to evolutionary psychology and neuroscience.

items.title: How can every physicist become a Bohmian
items.summary: The Bohmian interpretation of quantum mechanics is controversial because it attributes deterministic trajectories to microscopic particles. We propose a reformulation that sidesteps this controversy: rather than applying Bohmian mechanics at the microscopic level, we recast it as an effective deterministic description of the macroscopic pointer of a measuring apparatus, with no claims about the fundamental nature of the microscopic world. In this form, the Bohmian trajectory becomes a practical tool for visualizing the emergence of a definite measurement outcome, broadly acceptable to physicists who would otherwise reject the Bohmian program.
items.headline: How can every physicist become a Bohmian
items.brief: This article proposes a reformulation of the Bohmian interpretation of quantum mechanics by applying it at the macroscopic level of measurement apparatus pointers rather than at the microscopic particle level. This approach avoids controversial claims about microscopic determinism and instead uses Bohmian trajectories as practical tools to visualize how definite measurement outcomes emerge. The reformulation aims to make Bohmian mechanics more broadly acceptable to physicists by focusing on effective descriptions of measurement.
items.why: It offers a novel conceptual framework for interpreting quantum mechanics, relevant to foundational physics and the philosophy of science.
